title: Two in the desert (Bava Metzia 62a)
hook: one flask, two travelers; Rabbi Akiva teaches that your own life comes first

segments.voice: Yesterday Beruriah gave back what was entrusted. Your line was they were on loan. Did you treat something precious with care? Day two hundred eighty-five.

Every flight, the same speech. In case of a loss of cabin pressure, put on your own mask before helping others. The first time you hear it, it sounds almost selfish. Shouldn't you help the child first? Then you realize: if you pass out, you can't help anyone. The Talmud has a much older, much harder version of that same question. Two people are walking through the desert. Only one of them has water. And there isn't enough for two. Today, two sages disagree about what to do.
screen: `PUT ON YOUR OWN MASK FIRST.` → `TWO IN THE DESERT.` → `WATER ENOUGH FOR ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the case, in tractate Bava Metzia. Two people are traveling, and one has a flask of water. If both drink, both will die. If one drinks, he'll reach the next town alive. What should he do? A sage named Ben Petura taught: better that both drink and both die, than that one watch the other die. Share it, whatever happens. It's a beautiful, brave answer. Then Rabbi Akiva came and taught from a verse in Leviticus: "that thy brother may live with thee." With thee, Akiva said. Your brother lives with you, alongside you. So your own life comes first. The one with the flask may drink. Most later Jewish law follows Rabbi Akiva. Now, this isn't a license for selfishness. Look where the verse comes from: it's about lending to someone in need without charging interest, about keeping your brother alive. And look at the case: it's an extreme one, where sharing means certain death for both. Akiva isn't saying ignore other people. He's saying you're a person too. Your life counts in the math. Two thousand years later, the airline says the same thing in a calmer voice. You can't care for anyone if you've collapsed. Ben Petura's answer is still printed on the page, honored as a brave view. But the teaching that became the law is Akiva's: your life comes first, and then, with it, your brother's.
screen: `ONE FLASK, TWO TRAVELERS.` · `BEN PETURA: BOTH DRINK.` · `AKIVA: THAT HE MAY LIVE WITH THEE.` · `NOT SELFISH: YOU COUNT TOO.` · then, large: `YOUR LIFE COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check your own flask. Settle, and breathe. Where are you running low right now? Sleep, food, quiet, time with friends, a doctor's appointment you keep putting off. Notice who depends on you. Now notice that they depend on you being alive and well. Pick one small thing that would refill your flask today. Water. A walk. Going to bed on time. Picture doing it, not as a treat, but as part of caring for them. The bell holds the time.
Two in the desert. With one flask between them, Rabbi Akiva taught: your life comes first, and your brother lives with you.
Your line: your life comes first. Today, do one thing that refills your own flask, so you have something to give. Day two hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Jewish ethics takes care of one's own health seriously, and Akiva's ruling, chayekha kodmin, your life comes first, is still discussed in debates about triage and self-sacrifice.
